title: What SLAM is, and the math you need
days: D1 (already written, see src/w01/d1.html): §I.1–I.2, pp. 3–8. What SLAM is, front-end vs back-end, landmark-based vs pose-graph, drift and loop closure
D2: §I.3, pp. 9–13 (SLAM in the autonomy architecture, do we need SLAM?) + probability warm-up: random variables, Gaussians (1-D and multivariate), Bayes' rule, MLE vs MAP

D3: §I.4–I.5, pp. 13–18 (history: EKF → particle filters → factor graphs; SLAM to Spatial AI; handbook structure) + fusing two Gaussians, covariance form vs information form (why the information matrix is the natural object)
D4: no new book pages (re-read the Notation pages xiv–xv). Linear least squares: residuals, normal equations, weighted least squares as Gaussian maximum likelihood, Mahalanobis norm
D5: no new book pages. Matrix factorizations you will need all course: Cholesky, QR, SVD, positive definiteness, condition number, why you never invert a matrix explicitly
extra: Gaussians, Bayes/MAP, least squares, QR/Cholesky/SVD
widgets: MAIN: Gaussian fusion (1-D prior × measurement → posterior; 2-D ellipses fused in information form). Also good: a line-fit least-squares demo with draggable points and weights; condition-number demo.

title: Factor graphs and nonlinear least squares
days: D1: §1.1, pp. 19–24. The toy example, Bayes net vs factor graph, factor graphs as a language
D2: §1.2, pp. 25–28. MAP inference on factor graphs, Gaussian measurement and motion models, from MAP to nonlinear least squares
D3: §1.3, pp. 29–32. Linearization, SLAM as linear least squares, solving by Cholesky and QR
D4: §1.4.1–1.4.2, pp. 33–34. Steepest descent and Gauss-Newton, derived from the Taylor expansion
D5: §1.4.3–1.4.4, pp. 34–35. Levenberg-Marquardt and Powell's dogleg as trust-region methods
extra: Deriving Gauss-Newton and LM from Taylor expansion, trust regions, why GN is Newton without the second-order term
widgets: MAIN: 2-D pose-graph optimizer (a small loop of poses with noisy odometry + one loop closure; step through gradient descent vs Gauss-Newton vs LM and plot the cost per iteration). Also good: toy bearing/range example builder showing the factor graph; 1-D nonlinear least squares where GN overshoots and LM damps.

title: Sparsity, elimination, and incremental SLAM
days: D1: §1.5, pp. 35–39. Sparse Jacobian ↔ factor graph, information matrix ↔ Markov random field, sparse factorization
D2: §1.6.1–1.6.2, pp. 40–44. Variable elimination, linear-Gaussian elimination as partial QR
D3: §1.6.3 + ordering, pp. 44–46. Sparse Cholesky factor as a Bayes net, fill-in and variable ordering (COLAMD idea), Schur complement and marginalization
D4: §1.7.1–1.7.2, pp. 46–49. Bayes tree, cliques, updating only the affected part
D5: §1.7.3–1.8, pp. 49–52. iSAM/iSAM2, fluid relinearization, further reading
extra: Schur complement, marginalization vs conditioning of Gaussians (covariance and information form), fill-in
widgets: MAIN: factor graph ↔ Jacobian pattern ↔ information matrix pattern for a small SLAM problem, with step-through elimination under a chosen variable ordering that shows fill-in and the resulting Bayes net. Also good: Schur-complement marginalization of one variable from a 3-variable Gaussian.

title: Lie groups and optimization on manifolds
days: D1: §2.1.1, pp. 53–55. Rotations and poses, why SO(3)/SE(3) are not vector spaces, constraints and degrees of freedom
D2: §2.1.2, pp. 55–56. Matrix Lie groups, Lie algebra, wedge/vee, Exp/Log; derive Rodrigues' formula from the series
D3: §2.1.3, pp. 57–58. Perturbations, the ⊕ operator, linearizing a measurement model on SE(3), Gauss-Newton on a manifold (the PnP example)
D4: §2.1.4, pp. 59–60. Uncertainty on Lie groups: Gaussians in the tangent space, propagating covariance through composition
D5: §2.1.5, pp. 60–61. Adjoint, left/right Jacobians of SO(3), BCH formula, interpolation
extra: Rodrigues formula derivation, adjoint, BCH, SO(3) left/right Jacobians, quaternions vs rotation matrices
widgets: MAIN: Exp/Log playground on SO(2)/SE(2): sliders for a tangent vector, show the group element, the screw-like motion path, and that Exp(a)Exp(b) ≠ Exp(a+b). Also MAIN: 'banana' distribution — sample Gaussian noise in the tangent space of SE(2), compose over many steps, and compare with the Gaussian-in-(x,y) ellipse.

title: Continuous-time trajectories: splines and Gaussian processes
days: D1: §2.2.1, pp. 62–65 (approx.). Why continuous time (high-rate and asynchronous sensors, rolling shutter); B-splines, basis functions, local support
D2: §2.2.2, from parametric to nonparametric: basis functions, kernels, the weight-space view
D3: §2.2.3, Gaussian processes: GP regression, priors from linear time-varying SDEs (white-noise-on-acceleration), why the inverse kernel matrix is sparse (Markov)
D4: §2.2.4, splines and GPs on Lie groups: cumulative B-splines, local variables
D5: §2.3 further reading (to p. 74) + a worked GP regression example by hand and interpolation at query times
extra: B-spline basis recursion, GP regression equations (posterior mean and covariance), SDE-driven GP priors and their sparse precision
widgets: MAIN: fit a 1-D/2-D trajectory to noisy, irregularly timed measurements with (a) a uniform cubic B-spline (drag control points or change knot spacing) and (b) a GP with a constant-velocity prior (change hyperparameters); show the posterior band. Also good: B-spline basis function viewer.

title: Outliers and robust estimation
days: D1: §3.1, pp. 75–77. Where outliers come from (data association), why least squares breaks: one outlier can move the estimate arbitrarily
D2: §3.2.1, pp. 78–81 (approx.). RANSAC, minimal solvers, how many iterations
D3: §3.2.2, to p. 84. Graph-theoretic outlier rejection, pairwise consistency maximization, maximum clique
D4: §3.3.1–3.3.2, pp. 85–91 (approx.). M-estimators and robust losses, IRLS, Black-Rangarajan duality
D5: §3.3.3–3.4, to p. 100. Alternating minimization, graduated non-convexity (GNC) for Geman-McClure and truncated least squares, further reading
extra: M-estimators, influence functions and weight functions, breakdown point, the RANSAC iteration count formula, Black-Rangarajan derivation
widgets: MAIN: robust line fitting with outliers — RANSAC animation (sample, score, keep best) vs least squares vs IRLS. MAIN: GNC — plot the surrogate cost as the control parameter μ varies and step the alternating weights/variables updates on a 1-D or line-fit problem. Also good: robust-loss gallery (ρ, influence, weight) and a pairwise-consistency graph.

title: Differentiable optimization
days: D1: §4.1 + intro, pp. 101–102. Why differentiate through an optimizer (learning front-ends end to end); primer on forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation
D2: §4.2.1–4.2.2, pp. 103–106 (approx.). Unrolled differentiation and truncated unrolling: memory and bias trade-offs
D3: §4.2.3, to p. 109. Implicit differentiation via the implicit function theorem; the linear system you solve
D4: §4.3, pp. 109–113. Lie group derivatives and differentiation on manifolds
D5: §4.4–4.5, pp. 113–118. Numerical challenges, an implementation example, libraries (Theseus, PyPose, etc.), further reading
extra: Implicit function theorem, forward vs reverse autodiff, adjoint method, bilevel optimization
widgets: MAIN: toy bilevel problem (inner problem: nonlinear least squares in x with parameter θ; outer loss on x*(θ)). Compare the gradient dL/dθ from unrolling K Gauss-Newton/gradient steps (slider K) against the implicit-differentiation gradient and a finite-difference reference. Also good: a tiny computation graph showing forward vs reverse mode passes.

title: Dense map representations
days: D1: §5.1, pp. 119–121. Range sensing, the beam measurement model, converting scans to point clouds
D2: §5.2, pp. 122–126. Occupancy maps (log-odds Bayesian update) and signed distance fields (TSDF, ESDF); when to use which
D3: §5.3, pp. 126–135. Map representations: explicit vs implicit, spatial abstractions, data structures (grids, octrees, hashing)
D4: §5.4, pp. 135–145. Constructing maps: points, surfels, meshes (marching cubes), voxels, Gaussian processes, Hilbert maps, learning-based
D5: §5.5, pp. 145–148. Choosing a representation for the environment and downstream task
extra: Deriving the log-odds occupancy update from Bayes' rule, signed distance and the Eikonal property, TSDF weighted averaging, marching squares/cubes
widgets: MAIN: a 2-D robot with a simulated lidar in a small world: move the robot, cast rays, and build (a) a log-odds occupancy grid and (b) a TSDF with weighted averaging; show the zero crossing. Also good: marching squares on a small SDF grid; quadtree/octree refinement.

title: Certifiably optimal SLAM: Shor's relaxation and SE-Sync
days: D1: chapter intro + §6.1 opening, pp. 149–151. Local minima in SLAM, what 'certifiable' means; primer on convex sets/functions and why convex problems are easy
D2: §6.1.1, pp. 152–154. QCQPs, the lifting X = xxᵀ, Shor's relaxation, the bound d* ≤ p*, when rank-1 means exact
D3: §6.1.2.1, pose-graph optimization as maximum likelihood and as a QCQP (eliminating translations, the rotation-only problem)
D4: §6.1.2.2, the SDP relaxation of PGO, Lagrangian duality, the certificate matrix, exactness under small noise
D5: §6.1.2.3 to p. 164. Solving the SDP at scale: low-rank (Burer-Monteiro) factorization, the Riemannian staircase, verification
extra: Convexity, Lagrangian duality, weak/strong duality, KKT, semidefinite programs, the Stiefel manifold
widgets: MAIN: angular synchronization on a small graph (a 2-D rotation-only pose graph). Run local search from random starts and show local minima; run the rank-r relaxation by Riemannian gradient descent (r slider: 2 = original problem, 3+ = relaxed), then form the certificate matrix S = Q − Λ and report its minimum eigenvalue (≥ 0 ⇒ certified global optimum). A noise slider shows where tightness breaks. Use M.eigSym. Also good: a 1-D/2-D picture of a non-convex QCQP and its relaxation bound.

title: Beyond pose graphs, and how accurate SLAM can be
days: D1: §6.1.3, pp. 165–168 (approx.). Certifiable landmark-based SLAM
D2: §6.1.4, to p. 173. Extensions: range measurements, anisotropic noise, outliers (certifiable robust estimation)
D3: §6.2.1, pp. 173–175. Cramér-Rao lower bound and the Fisher information matrix, with a proof sketch
D4: §6.2.2, pp. 175–178. Fisher information and the graph Laplacian: connectivity, spanning trees, why loop closures help
D5: §6.3, pp. 178–182. Further readings and recent trends
D6: review of Week 10 AND of all of Part I (Weeks 1–10): include a Part I concept map section and a longer mixed quiz (10 questions)
extra: Fisher information, CRLB proof sketch, graph Laplacian, algebraic connectivity, matrix-tree theorem (weighted number of spanning trees)
widgets: MAIN: a 2-D pose graph (translations only is fine, or with known rotations) where the user toggles loop-closure edges; show the reduced Laplacian, its eigenvalues (algebraic connectivity), the log-determinant / tree-connectivity, and the per-node covariance ellipses from the inverse of the Fisher information shrinking as edges are added. Also good: CRLB vs sample variance simulation for a simple estimator.

title: Visual SLAM I: cameras, features, and the pipeline
days: D1: Prelude II, pp. 185–192. Front-end modules (odometry, loop closure, priors), sensors as factors, fusion, calibration and synchronization, evaluation metrics (ATE/RPE)
D2: §7.1–7.2, pp. 193–197. History and terminology (photogrammetry, BA, SfM, VO, visual SLAM); the processing pipeline
D3: §7.3.1–7.3.3, pp. 197–201 (approx.). Camera model (pinhole, intrinsics, distortion), keypoints and descriptors, reprojection error
D4: §7.3.4–7.3.5. Keypoint-based visual SLAM and photometric error / direct methods
D5: §7.3.6–7.3.8, to p. 206. Place recognition (bag of words), initialization (two-view geometry, triangulation), map representations
extra: Homogeneous coordinates, projective geometry, the essential and fundamental matrices (derive the epipolar constraint), triangulation, PnP, ATE vs RPE
widgets: MAIN: two pinhole cameras looking at 3-D points (top-down + two image planes): move the second camera, click a point in image 1 to draw its epipolar line in image 2, and show the reprojection error as a point or camera is perturbed. Also good: triangulation uncertainty vs baseline; lens distortion slider.

title: Visual SLAM II: alignment, bundle adjustment, full systems
days: D1: §7.4.1, pp. 207–209 (approx.). Keypoint-based image alignment: PnP and motion-only BA, Jacobian of the reprojection error
D2: §7.4.2. Direct image alignment: photometric residuals, Lucas-Kanade as Gauss-Newton, coarse-to-fine pyramids
D3: §7.4.3. Solving BA: the arrow-shaped Hessian, the Schur complement trick, reduced camera system
D4: §7.4.4, to p. 214. BA revisited: gauge freedom, marginalization, sliding windows, keyframes
D5: §7.5–7.9, pp. 215–223. Example systems (e.g., ORB-SLAM, DSO), dense reconstruction, depth cameras, fusing IMU/GPS/WiFi, trends
extra: Lucas-Kanade derivation, Schur complement trick in BA, gauge freedom (7 DoF monocular), inverse-depth parameterization
widgets: MAIN: mini bundle adjustment in 2-D (cameras on a line/arc observing landmarks with 1-D bearing 'images'): show the Hessian sparsity (camera block, point block, coupling), apply the Schur complement step by step, and iterate Gauss-Newton with noise. MAIN 2: 1-D direct alignment (Lucas-Kanade) of a shifted intensity profile with a pyramid toggle showing the basin of convergence.

title: LiDAR SLAM
days: D1: §8.1, pp. 224–226. How LiDARs work, sensor types, scan patterns, motion distortion
D2: §8.2.1, pp. 227–231 (approx.). Scan registration foundations: ICP, closed-form rigid alignment by SVD, point-to-plane, GICP, NDT
D3: §8.2.2–8.2.3, to p. 235. Components of LiDAR odometry (deskewing, feature extraction, local maps, LiDAR-inertial coupling) and summary of systems
D4: §8.3, pp. 236–239. LiDAR place recognition: global descriptors (e.g., Scan Context), learning-based methods
D5: §8.4–8.5, pp. 240–249. Full LiDAR SLAM: pose-graph optimization, map update, multi-robot and multi-session, trends
extra: Closed-form rigid alignment (Kabsch/Umeyama via SVD) derivation, point-to-plane linearization, GICP as distribution-to-distribution, NDT
widgets: MAIN: 2-D ICP step-through: two scans of the same shape, choose point-to-point or point-to-plane, step correspondences → alignment → repeat, plot the error, and show a bad initial guess converging to a local minimum. Also good: a ring/sector polar descriptor (Scan-Context-like) that is compared under rotation by column shift.

title: Radar SLAM
days: D1: §9.1.1–9.1.2, pp. 250–256 (approx.). Radar sensor types (spinning vs SoC), FMCW principle, range and Doppler
D2: §9.1.3–9.1.4, to p. 260. Challenges (speckle, multipath, sparsity) and filtering (CFAR)
D3: §9.2, pp. 261–268. Radar odometry: Doppler-based ego-velocity, direct, feature-based, registration-based; motion compensation
D4: §9.3, pp. 269–272. Radar place recognition
D5: §9.4–9.6, pp. 273–281. Radar SLAM pipelines, map representations, multi-modal fusion, datasets, trends
extra: FMCW beat frequency → range, phase across chirps → Doppler velocity, range/velocity resolution formulas, CFAR thresholding, ego-velocity least squares from radial velocities
widgets: MAIN: FMCW radar: sliders for target range/velocity and chirp bandwidth; show transmitted/received chirps, the beat signal, and its spectrum (a small DFT) with the range peak; second panel: CA-CFAR threshold on a noisy range profile. MAIN 2: Doppler ego-velocity: static points around a moving sensor produce a cosine of radial velocity vs azimuth; fit ego-velocity by least squares and reject moving-object outliers.

title: Event-based SLAM
days: D1: §10.1, pp. 282–285. How an event camera works: the event generation model, advantages, devices
D2: §10.2–10.3, pp. 286–288. Challenges, applications, taxonomy of event-based SLAM methods
D3: §10.4, pp. 289–292. Front-end: event representations (event frames, time surfaces, voxel grids), indirect vs direct, model-based vs learned
D4: §10.5–10.6, pp. 293–294, plus the app's deeper look at contrast maximization (motion compensation as an optimization problem)
D5: §10.7–10.8, pp. 294–303. Simulators, datasets, metrics, trends
extra: Event generation model (log-intensity threshold), linearized event generation (brightness constancy), contrast maximization objective
widgets: MAIN: event camera simulator: a moving edge/pattern across a 1-D or small 2-D sensor; contrast-threshold slider; show the events (polarity) in an x–t plot next to what a frame camera would capture (motion blur). MAIN 2: contrast maximization: warp events by a candidate velocity (slider) and plot the image-of-warped-events variance, which peaks at the true velocity. This is a lighter week: keep the lessons a little shorter.

title: Inertial sensing and IMU preintegration
days: D1: §11.1.1, pp. 304–306. Gyroscopes and accelerometers, the measurement model (bias, noise, gravity), specific force
D2: §11.1.2, pp. 306–308. Initial alignment (finding gravity, roll and pitch), noise parameters in practice (noise density, bias random walk)
D3: §11.2.1, pp. 308–311 (approx.). Motion integration: continuous kinematics, discrete integration, why re-integrating at every optimizer iteration is too expensive
D4: §11.2.2. IMU preintegration on the manifold: the relative-motion increments ΔR, Δv, Δp, noise propagation, the preintegration factor
D5: §11.2.3, to p. 318. Bias-correction Jacobians (first-order bias update), advanced preintegration techniques
extra: Strapdown kinematics, noise models (white noise + bias random walk, Allan variance idea), derivation of ΔR/Δv/Δp independence from the initial state and gravity, covariance propagation
widgets: MAIN: 2-D IMU dead reckoning: a vehicle on a known path with simulated gyro+accelerometer; sliders for noise and bias; show position error growing roughly quadratically/cubically and how a small gyro bias tilts 'gravity' into horizontal acceleration. MAIN 2: preintegration: change the initial velocity/orientation and show that the preintegrated increment between two keyframes is unchanged while naive integration must be redone.

title: Observability and visual-inertial odometry
days: D1: §11.3.1, pp. 319–321. Linearized measurement models and the error-state system
D2: §11.3.2, pp. 321–324. Observability analysis: the observability matrix, its nullspace, the four unobservable directions of VIO (global position and yaw)
D3: §11.3.3, pp. 324–326. Degenerate motions (constant acceleration, pure translation, no rotation) and what becomes unobservable
D4: §11.4.1, pp. 326–328. Visual-inertial odometry: filtering (MSCKF) vs optimization, consistency and first-estimates Jacobians
D5: §11.4.2–11.5, pp. 328–332. Extrinsic calibration, temporal synchronization, further reading
extra: Observability for linear systems (rank test), unobservable subspace as the nullspace, gauge freedom vs observability, why estimator inconsistency appears (FEJ)
widgets: MAIN: observability lab: a 2-D camera+IMU-like toy system where the user picks the motion (constant velocity, constant acceleration, varying acceleration, with/without rotation); compute the numerical observability/information matrix, show its eigenvalues with M.eigSym, and draw the unobservable directions (scale, global translation, yaw) as motions of the whole solution. Also good: monocular scale ambiguity demo (scaling scene and trajectory leaves images unchanged).

title: Leg odometry, and Part II in review
days: D1: §12.1.1–12.1.3, pp. 333–337 (approx.). History, reference frames, state definition for a legged robot
D2: §12.1.4–12.1.6, to p. 341. Forward kinematics, the leg Jacobian, floating-base dynamics, joint sensing (encoders, torque)
D3: §12.2, pp. 342–344. Motion estimation: relative pose from stance feet, velocity estimation
D4: §12.3, pp. 345–347. Contact estimation: contact sensors, force/torque sensors, IMUs, joint torques
D5: §12.4–12.6, pp. 348–358. Encoder noise propagation, factor-graph smoothing with leg odometry, fusing with exteroceptive sensors, open challenges (deformation, slip)
D6: review of Week 18 AND of all of Part II (Weeks 11–18): include a sensor comparison table and a longer mixed quiz (10 questions)
extra: Forward kinematics of a planar leg, Jacobians (foot velocity from joint rates), the zero-velocity stance-foot constraint, how slip breaks it
widgets: MAIN: a planar 2-link leg (or a biped with alternating stance legs): joint-angle sliders or a gait play button; compute body motion from the stance-foot constraint with encoder noise and a slip slider; show estimated vs true body trajectory drifting. Also good: contact detection from a simulated ground-reaction force with a threshold.

title: Boosting SLAM with deep learning
days: D1: Prelude III, pp. 361–365 + Ch 13 intro, pp. 366–368. Spatial AI and its applications; where learning enters the SLAM pipeline
D2: §13.1, pp. 368–373. Learning depth and camera pose (supervised and self-supervised via photometric reprojection)
D3: §13.2, pp. 374–378. Learned features and matching (SuperPoint/SuperGlue-style), optical flow and RAFT (correlation volumes, iterative updates)
D4: §13.3, pp. 379–385. Differentiable bundle adjustment, DROID-SLAM, DPVO
D5: §13.4–13.7, pp. 386–396. DUSt3R pointmaps and the confidence-aware loss, MASt3R, MASt3R-SfM/MUSt3R/MASt3R-SLAM, open challenges
extra: Short primer on CNNs/transformers/attention as needed, self-supervised photometric loss, correlation volume lookup, the dense BA layer as weighted Gauss-Newton with learned confidence weights, pointmaps and scale ambiguity
widgets: MAIN: RAFT-style matching in 1-D/2-D: two small feature rows/images, build the correlation volume (heat map), and iterate 'lookup → update' steps that refine the flow estimate. MAIN 2: confidence-weighted alignment: residuals with learned-style weights where down-weighting bad matches changes the Gauss-Newton solution (links to Week 6). This is a page-heavy week (36 pp.): keep derivations focused.

title: NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting as maps
days: D1: chapter intro + §14.1, pp. 397–400. Learnable 3-D representations and differentiable rendering
D2: §14.2.1, pp. 401–404 (approx.). NeRF: the volume rendering integral and its quadrature, positional encoding, hierarchical sampling
D3: §14.2.2–14.2.4, to p. 408. Data structures (voxel grids, hash grids, tri-planes), neural fields beyond radiance (SDF), NeRF-based SLAM
D4: §14.3.1, pp. 409–412 (approx.). 3D Gaussian splatting: Gaussian primitives, projection to 2-D (EWA), alpha compositing, densification
D5: §14.3.2–14.4, to p. 416. Gaussian-splatting SLAM, applications, trends
extra: Deriving the discrete volume rendering weights from the continuous integral (transmittance, alpha), projecting a 3-D Gaussian covariance through the camera Jacobian, front-to-back alpha compositing
widgets: MAIN: a single camera ray through an editable density profile: show σ(t), transmittance T(t), per-sample α and weights, and the rendered colour/depth; slider for number of samples. MAIN 2: 2-D Gaussian splatting: a few coloured anisotropic Gaussians projected onto a 1-D image and alpha-composited front to back; drag Gaussians or change opacity and watch the image change (optionally one gradient step toward a target image).

title: Dynamic and deformable SLAM
days: D1: chapter intro + §15.1, pp. 417–422. Characterizing dynamics (short-term vs long-term, rigid vs deformable), estimation vs representation, online vs offline
D2: §15.2, pp. 423–431. Short-term dynamics: dynamic object removal, object tracking with motion factors, dense dynamic SLAM
D3: §15.3.1–15.3.2, pp. 432–438 (approx.). Lifelong SLAM for localization, map cleaning and change detection
D4: §15.3.3–15.3.4, to p. 445. Change-aware SLAM and temporal scene understanding
D5: §15.4–15.5, pp. 446–453. Deformable SLAM: NRSfM vs deformable SLAM, with depth, monocular pipeline, initialization; trends
extra: Free-space ray-casting for dynamic point removal, object-motion factors in a factor graph (rigid-body SE(3) motion), deformation graphs / as-rigid-as-possible regularization
widgets: MAIN: a 2-D lidar world with a moving object: compare naive point accumulation (ghost trail) against occupancy/free-space filtering that clears the trail; sliders for object speed and a hit/miss update strength. Also good: a deformation-graph toy (drag one node of a mesh and regularize the rest as-rigid-as-possible), or tracking a moving object with a constant-velocity motion factor.

title: Metric-semantic SLAM
days: D1: chapter intro + §16.1 + first half of §16.2.1, pp. 454–460 (approx.). From geometric to metric-semantic maps; object landmarks (points, cuboids, quadrics) and semantic factors
D2: rest of §16.2.1 + §16.2.2, to p. 470. Discrete-continuous factor graphs, semantic data association, hybrid solvers (EM, max-mixtures, discrete-continuous optimization)
D3: §16.3, pp. 471–481. Dense metric-semantic maps: point/surfel, voxel (Bayesian label fusion), mesh
D4: §16.4, pp. 482–486. Hierarchical representations, 3-D scene graphs, symbol grounding
D5: §16.5, pp. 487–489 + worked examples on expectation-maximization and max-mixture data association
extra: Discrete-continuous inference, EM for data association, max-mixture factors, Bayesian categorical label fusion (log-probability accumulation)
widgets: MAIN: ambiguous semantic data association: a robot observes several look-alike object landmarks with noisy class labels; compare nearest-neighbour hard association, max-mixture, and EM soft association on a small 2-D problem, showing association weights. MAIN 2: a small 3-D scene graph browser (building → rooms → objects) where a text-like query traverses the hierarchy; plus Bayesian label fusion for one voxel as observations arrive.

title: Open-world spatial AI and foundation models
days: D1: chapter intro + §17.1, pp. 490–494. A brief history of foundation models, terminology: closed-set vs open-vocabulary
D2: §17.2, pp. 495–498. Feature-based models (CLIP, DINO), generative models (LLMs, VLMs), class-agnostic segmentation (SAM)
D3: §17.3.1–17.3.2, pp. 499–507 (approx.). Open-world mapping: dense feature maps, object maps and open-vocabulary 3-D scene graphs
D4: §17.3.3–17.3.4, to p. 513. Implicit functions (feature fields) and task-driven representations
D5: §17.4, pp. 514–520. Grounding foundation models with maps, do we still need maps?, a foundation model for robotics?
extra: Contrastive learning objective (InfoNCE) behind CLIP, cosine similarity in a joint embedding space, fusing per-pixel features into a 3-D map by weighted averaging
widgets: MAIN: open-vocabulary query on a toy map: a small 2-D grid map whose cells hold low-dimensional 'embedding' vectors (hand-built so that related concepts are close); choose a query word and a threshold to see cosine-similarity heat and the retrieved region; show how multi-view averaging of noisy features sharpens it. Also good: a contrastive-loss toy showing a similarity matrix being pulled toward the diagonal.

title: The computational structure of Spatial AI, and the whole course in review
days: D1: §18.1–18.2, pp. 521–525. From SLAM to Spatial AI, scene representation and world models, the overall computational structure
D2: §18.3–18.4, pp. 526–531. State estimation and machine learning together; the future of processors and sensors
D3: §18.5, pp. 532–539. Mapping Spatial AI graphs to hardware: world-model processing, the real-time loop, processing near the image plane
D4: §18.6–18.7, pp. 540–544. Gaussian belief propagation as convergent distributed computation; continual learning within factor graphs
D5: §18.8–18.9 + Epilogue, pp. 545–550. Performance metrics, trends, and the editors' closing view
D6: review of Week 24, of Part III (Weeks 19–24), AND a whole-course wrap-up: a one-page concept map from factor graphs to Spatial AI, a 12-question mixed quiz, and 'where to go next'
extra: Gaussian belief propagation message-passing equations in information form (derive variable-to-factor and factor-to-variable messages), relation to elimination from Week 3
widgets: MAIN: Gaussian belief propagation on a 1-D pose chain with a loop closure (or a small 2-D grid): step message passing one iteration at a time, show each variable's belief (mean ± σ) converging to the exact least-squares solution computed with M.solve; options for synchronous vs random schedules and a robust-factor toggle.
